config.title: Type a todo CRUD app with strict models

intro.title: Type a todo CRUD app with strict models
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple todo list application where you can create, read, update, and delete tasks. You will learn how to use TypeScript's type system to define strict models for your todo data, ensuring each task has a consistent structure. The main technologies involved are TypeScript interfaces and types to enforce these models. By the end, you'll understand how strong typing helps prevent errors and makes your code more predictable and maintainable.
intro.usecase: This pattern is essential for building any interactive data management interface, such as admin dashboards, customer relationship management (CRM) systems, or project management tools like Trello or Asana. For example, in a project management app, you need strict models to create, read, update, and delete tasks, ensuring data consistency across views like task lists, detail panels, and modal forms. As a developer, implementing typed CRUD operations prevents runtime errors, improves code maintainability, and provides clear interfaces for team collaboration, directly mirroring real-world scenarios where user data must be handled reliably and predictably.

objectives: Construct a strict TypeScript interface to model a todo item with required properties
Initialize a state variable with the correct type annotation to store an array of todo items
Implement a function to add new todo items while enforcing type constraints
Apply type-safe logic to toggle the completion status of existing todo items
Manipulate the todo array to remove items using proper TypeScript array methods
Render the todo list in the UI by mapping over the typed state array
Configure event handlers to trigger CRUD operations with type-checked parameters

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: At the top of your file, write the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have the necessary imports to start building your todo app with state management.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'. Check your import statement syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import React and useState from 'react' to proceed with the lesson.

steps.title: Define the Todo interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named 'Todo' with three properties: 'id' as a number, 'text' as a string, and 'completed' as a boolean.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions inside curly braces.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Define the Todo interface here
steps.expectedOutcome: A Todo interface is created with the correct property types, providing a strict model for todo items.
successCriteria: The Todo interface is defined with id: number, text: string, and completed: boolean properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the interface needs all three properties with the correct types. Make sure you have id (number), text (string), and completed (boolean).
steps.feedbackWrong: The Todo interface isn't defined correctly. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword and define all three properties with their types.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function called App. It should return JSX, such as a simple div or heading for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns JSX.
successCriteria: A functional component named App is created and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component is named exactly 'App' and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component is not defined correctly. Check the component name and that it returns JSX.

steps.title: Initialize state with todos array
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, initialize a state variable named 'todos' using useState, typed as Todo[], with an initial value of an empty array.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with the generic type Todo[] to ensure TypeScript knows todos will be an array of Todo objects.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: typed state array
const [items, setItems] = useState<string[]>([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The todos state variable is declared with the correct type and initial empty array.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with Todo[] as its generic type and [] as the initial value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the Todo[] type and providing an empty array as the initial value.
steps.feedbackWrong: use useState with the Todo[] type and initialize it with an empty array.

steps.title: Define the addTodo handler
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named addTodo that takes a string parameter called text, creates a new Todo object, and updates the todos state.
steps.hint: The function should create a new todo object with a unique id, the provided text, and completed set to false, then add it to the existing todos array using the setTodos state setter.
steps.expectedOutcome: The addTodo function is defined inside the component, ready to be called with new todo text.
successCriteria: A function named addTodo is defined that takes a string parameter, creates a Todo object with id, text, and completed properties, and updates the todos state using setTodos.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function creates a complete Todo object and properly updates the state array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The addTodo function isn't defined correctly. Check that it takes a string parameter, creates a Todo object, and updates the state.

steps.title: Define the deleteTodo handler
steps.instruction: Define a function named deleteTodo that takes a todo id (type number) and removes that todo from the todos state array.
steps.hint: Use the setTodos updater function with the .filter method to create a new array excluding the todo with the matching id.
steps.expectedOutcome: A deleteTodo function is defined inside the App component, ready to be called with a todo id to remove that todo.
successCriteria: The deleteTodo function is defined, takes a number parameter (id), and uses setTodos with .filter to update the state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function takes an id parameter of type number and uses setTodos with .filter to remove the matching todo.
steps.feedbackWrong: The deleteTodo function is not correctly defined. It should take a number id and use setTodos with .filter to create a new array without that todo.

steps.title: Add the main container structure
steps.instruction: In the App component's return statement, replace the current return value with a JSX structure: return a div element containing an h1 heading with the text 'Todo App' and an empty unordered list element.
steps.hint: The return statement should output JSX. Use a div as the root container, with an h1 inside it for the heading, and a ul element for the todo list container.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now returns a JSX structure with a heading and an empty list container, ready to display todo items.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a div with an h1 heading 'Todo App' and an empty ul element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your return statement includes both the h1 heading with 'Todo App' and an empty ul element inside a div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The return statement should output JSX with a div containing an h1 heading 'Todo App' and an empty ul element. Check your syntax and structure.

steps.title: Add input and button for adding todos
steps.instruction: Inside the main container, add an input field and a button labeled 'Add'. The button's onClick should call addTodo with the input's current value.
steps.hint: Use the <input> element for text input and <button> for the button. You'll need to get the input's value when the button is clicked.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will have a text input and an 'Add' button inside the container. Clicking the button will trigger the addTodo function.
successCriteria: An <input> element and a <button> with label 'Add' are present inside the container. The button's onClick calls addTodo with the input value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure both the input and button are inside the container, and the button's onClick calls addTodo.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input and button aren't set up correctly. Check that they're inside the container and the button triggers addTodo.

steps.title: Display the list of todos
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's return statement, map over the todos array to display each todo's text and completed status in an unordered list.
steps.hint: Use the map method on the todos array to generate a list item for each todo. Display the todo's text and completed status.
steps.expectedOutcome: The todos array is rendered as a list where each todo's text and completion status are displayed.
successCriteria: An unordered list is rendered that maps over the todos state, displaying each todo's text and completed status with a unique key.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started displaying the todos, but make sure to include both the text and completed status for each todo.
steps.feedbackWrong: The todos list is not displayed correctly. Ensure you are mapping over the todos array and rendering list items with the todo's text and completed status.

steps.title: Add toggle and delete buttons for each todo
steps.instruction: Inside the existing <li> element for each todo, add a 'Toggle' button with an onClick handler that calls toggleTodo(todo.id) and a 'Delete' button with an onClick handler that calls deleteTodo(todo.id).
steps.hint: Add two <button> elements inside the <li> after the todo text. Use onClick={() => toggleTodo(todo.id)} and onClick={() => deleteTodo(todo.id)}.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding interactive buttons to a list item
  • Item text
steps.expectedOutcome: Each todo item in the list will have two buttons: 'Toggle' to mark it as completed/pending and 'Delete' to remove it.
successCriteria: Each <li> contains a 'Toggle' button with onClick calling toggleTodo(todo.id) and a 'Delete' button with onClick calling deleteTodo(todo.id).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some buttons, but make sure each todo item has both a 'Toggle' and a 'Delete' button with the correct onClick handlers.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are missing or incorrectly placed. Each todo item should have a 'Toggle' button and a 'Delete' button inside the <li> element.

steps.title: Add type safety to input handling
steps.instruction: Add a local state variable for the input value with proper typing, and create an onChange handler for the input with correct TypeScript event typing.
steps.hint: Use useState<string> for the input value. The onChange handler should receive a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> and update the state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a typed input value state and a properly typed onChange handler, ensuring type safety for user input.
successCriteria: A useState<string> hook is added for input value, and an onChange handler with React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> typing is defined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both the state variable and event handler have proper TypeScript types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input handling doesn't have proper TypeScript typing. Remember to use useState<string> for the value and React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> for the event parameter.
